The "Fixing Communism" Sandbox: Solving the Incentive & Information Problem

The biggest failure of classic, Soviet-style communism wasn't just a lack of moral incentive; it was a data processing failure. In a market, prices act as a massive, decentralized routing system telling producers what to make and where to send it. When a state tries to calculate those billions of daily transactions manually, the system crashes.

1. CyberSyn (The Historical Sandbox)

In the early 1970s, Chile actually built a physical, real-time economic sandbox called Project CyberSyn. Designed by British cyberneticist Stafford Beer, it was a decentralized, computer-driven network meant to manage the national economy.

  • The Blueprint: It featured a futuristic operations room with data feeds coming from factories. If a factory ran low on materials or production stalled, an automated alert was triggered.
  • The Goal: It aimed to give workers autonomy at the local level (preserving initiative) while using computers to handle the massive calculation problem of resource allocation from the top, bypassing a clunky bureaucracy. It was cut short by a military coup in 1973, remaining one of history's great "what-ifs" of digital economic design.

2. Multi-Agent AI Simulation (The Modern Sandbox)

Today, computer scientists run economic sandboxes using Agent-Based Modeling (ABM). Instead of predicting human behavior with broad math, they program thousands of individual AI "agents" with specific traits, needs, and resource constraints, then let them trade in a closed digital environment.

  • The Experiment: Researchers use these to test things like "Market Socialism" (where firms are owned by the workers or the state, but still compete against each other in a market).
  • The Finding: The sandbox shows that if you reward agents based on the collective output of their local node (like a worker-owned cooperative) rather than a flat state wage, individual effort stays high, but the runaway wealth accumulation of pure capitalism is heavily blunted.

The "Fixing Capitalism" Sandbox: Taming the Monopolistic Weeds

To fix the "dark incentive" of capitalism—where the natural end-state of free competition is often a monopoly that devours its rivals—plenty of blueprints focus on changing the foundational rules of property and currency without getting rid of the market entirely.

1. Radical Markets & Harberger Taxes

Developed by economist Glen Weyl and legal scholar Eric Posner, this blueprint treats private property less like an unassailable fortress and more like a fluid, shared resource.

  • The Rule: You can own an asset (like land, a patent, or a factory), but you must publicly list its price at all times and pay a self-assessed tax on that value (say, 2%). The catch? Anyone can buy that asset from you at any time for your listed price.
  • Why it kills the "Weed": If a monopoly tries to hoard vital resources or land to choke out competitors, they have to self-assess a massive value to keep people from buying it, resulting in a crushing tax bill. If they under-report the value to save on taxes, a competitor will instantly buy it out from under them. It forces capital to stay productive and fluid.

2. Demurrage Currencies (The "Rotting" Money Sandbox)

In standard capitalism, hoarding money breeds more money through interest, which accelerates inequality. German-Argentine economist Silvio Gesell proposed a sandbox feature called demurrage.

  • The Rule: Money has an expiration date or a carrying cost. If you hold onto a dollar bill (or digital token) for too long without spending or investing it, it loses value—essentially "rotting" like food.
  • Why it alters incentive: It flips the incentive from hoarding wealth to circulating it. Wealthy actors can't just sit on massive piles of capital to choke out the market; they are forced to constantly invest it back into real-world, productive projects, leveling the playing field for smaller creators.

Simulating the Balance

Because testing these systems on a live population is incredibly risky, the best way to visualize how these adjustments play out is through parameter-driven models.

The interactive simulator below demonstrates the core mechanic of your "weed" analogy: how wealth distribution behaves over time under a standard capitalist model (where wealth generates more wealth) versus a regulated model using mechanisms like wealth caps or redistribution to simulate a balanced system.

These conceptual frameworks mostly live in academic papers, economic code repositories, or localized experiments (like specific cooperative networks or local currencies). They remain "vaulted" because transitioning a massive legacy economy to a completely new set of rules introduces massive friction—but the blueprints are ready for when the current systems hit a breaking point.
